Construct a Quadratic Penalty

Source: R/quadratic_penalty.R
quadratic_penalty.Rd

Builds the penalty \(\tfrac{\lambda}{2}(D\beta)'P(D\beta)\) together with the constant that makes it a density, so the value returned is exactly the negative log-density of the Gaussian prior with precision \(\lambda D'PD\). This is the penalty of a spline smooth, a ridge and a Gaussian random effect: one fixed matrix that weights the directions of the coefficients, and one smoothing parameter that scales the weights.

Usage

quadratic_penalty(
  P,
  map = NULL,
  blocks = 1L,
  link_lambda = linkfunctions7::log_link(),
  tol = 1e-10
)

Arguments

P

A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix, for instance a basis7 Gram matrix or a difference penalty \(D_k'D_k\). A matrix with an entry that is not finite (NA, NaN or infinite) is rejected. Symmetry is checked to a tolerance of 1e-8 times the larger of 1 and the largest absolute entry of P, and the matrix is symmetrized before use. A matrix whose largest eigenvalue is not positive (a zero or negative semidefinite matrix) is rejected, and so is one with an eigenvalue below -tol times the largest.

map

The matrix \(D\), with as many rows as \(P\) and one column per coefficient, or NULL (the default) for the identity, and then n_coef is nrow(P). A Matrix object keeps its own storage. A map with an entry that is not finite is rejected, and so is a map for which \(D'PD\) has no positive eigenvalue; a map that annihilates \(P\) only up to rounding is not detected (see the details).

blocks

How many times \(P\) is repeated blockwise, a whole number of at least 1. 1L, the default, is the ordinary single-block penalty. Above 1 it must be given without a map.

link_lambda

The linkfunctions7 link carrying \(\lambda\) onto the whole real line. The default is linkfunctions7::log_link(), because \(\lambda\) is positive.

tol

The relative eigenvalue tolerance of the rank rule, 1e-10 by default. An eigenvalue of \(D'PD\) at or below tol times the largest counts as zero, so its direction joins the null space and is not penalized. The same tolerance bounds the negative eigenvalues of \(P\) that are accepted as rounding errors. The object stores tol, and check_penalty() counts the rank at the same tolerance.

Value

A QuadraticPenalty() object with one hyperparameter, lambda, bounded on \((0, \infty)\).

The value

With \(r\) the rank of \(D'PD\),

$$\rho(\beta; \lambda) = \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\,(D\beta)'P(D\beta) - \tfrac{r}{2}\log\lambda + \tfrac{r}{2}\log 2\pi - \tfrac{1}{2}\log\mathrm{pdet}(D'PD).$$

The last three terms are the normalizing constant of the prior, taken only over the range of \(D'PD\) when that matrix is rank deficient. The constant is the one of the matrix applied to \(\beta\), so it carries the map. For a diagonal map with non-zero entries \(d_j\) and a full-rank \(P\), \(\log\mathrm{pdet}(D'PD) = \log\det P + 2\sum_j\log\lvert d_j\rvert\), and \(\sum_j\log\lvert d_j\rvert\) is the log Jacobian of \(\beta \mapsto D\beta\). The value is then the negative log-density of a proper Gaussian prior on \(\beta\), and a marginal criterion built on it does not change when a covariate is multiplied by a factor and the map multiplies the coefficient of that covariate by the same factor. The constant also makes \(\lambda\) estimable from a joint objective: without the term \(-\tfrac{r}{2}\log\lambda\) the penalty decreases to zero with \(\lambda\), and the joint maximum moves to the boundary \(\lambda \to 0\).

The rank and the null basis

The rank is counted at construction by the relative rule \(\mathrm{ev} > \mathtt{tol} \cdot \max(\mathrm{ev})\) on the eigenvalues of \(D'PD\), and the same mask selects the orthonormal null basis among the eigenvectors, so the null basis always has \(q - r\) columns, with \(q\) the number of coefficients. Without a map the eigenvalues come from a values-only decomposition of \(P\) and the eigenvectors from a second decomposition of the same matrix; both are sorted in decreasing order, so the mask selects the matching columns. With a map the rank, the log pseudo-determinant and the null basis all come from the decomposition of \(D'PD\).

Fixing the rank on each matrix keeps it stable when quadratic penalties are combined. A rank recounted from an assembled sum of several penalties falls as their smoothing parameters spread apart, while the true null space is the intersection of the null spaces of the components and does not depend on the smoothing parameters.

The rule is relative to the largest eigenvalue of \(D'PD\) itself. A map that annihilates \(P\) only up to rounding, so that every entry of \(D'PD\) is a rounding error relative to \(P\), is therefore not detected: the largest of those rounding errors passes the rule, and the penalty is built with a positive rank and a log pseudo-determinant made of rounding errors. The constructor rejects the map only when \(D'PD\) has no positive eigenvalue, as when \(D'PD\) is exactly the zero matrix.

Blockwise repetition

blocks = m builds the penalty of \(I_m \otimes P\) from \(P\) alone, which is the form that one copy of a smooth per level of a factor takes. The eigenvalues of \(I_m \otimes P\) are those of \(P\) repeated \(m\) times, so the rank is \(mr\), the log pseudo-determinant is \(m\log\mathrm{pdet}(P)\) and the null space is \(I_m \otimes N\), with \(N\) the null basis of \(P\). Only \(P\) is decomposed, and the large matrix is stored in sparse form. The result has the same value, gradient, Hessian, rank, null basis and log pseudo-determinant as the penalty built from the assembled \(I_m \otimes P\), up to rounding.

Under blocks > 1 the matrix-valued returns are dgCMatrix, not base matrices: penalty_hessian(), penalty_matrix(), penalty_null_basis() and the matrices of penalty_dhessian() all keep the sparse storage, so the assembled matrix is never densified. A consumer that writes these results into a block of its own information matrix has to accept both classes.

blocks does not combine with map, and the constructor rejects the pair: a map mixes the blocks, so \(D'(I_m \otimes P)D\) is in general not block diagonal and does not have the structure that blocks builds.

See also

additive_penalty() for a sum of quadratics with a smoothing parameter each, structured_penalty() for a matrix that moves with several hyperparameters, distrib_penalty() for the separable branch, penalty_logpdet() for the constant that a marginal criterion reads, check_penalty() to verify the result.

Examples

# Second differences over five coefficients: rank 3, and a null space
# holding the straight lines, so this is an improper prior.
P <- crossprod(diff(diag(5), differences = 2))
pen <- quadratic_penalty(P)
penalty_rank(pen)
#> [1] 3
is_proper(pen)
#> [1] FALSE

# A straight line lies in the null space and has zero gradient.
penalty_gradient(pen, c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), list(lambda = 2))
#> [1] 0 0 0 0 0

# A full-rank penalty is a proper Gaussian prior, and its value is the
# negative log-density of one.
ridge <- quadratic_penalty(diag(3))
b <- c(0.4, -1.1, 0.7)
all.equal(penalty_value(ridge, b, list(lambda = 2)),
          -sum(stats::dnorm(b, sd = 1 / sqrt(2), log = TRUE)))
#> [1] TRUE

# A map penalizes its image. Here only the second differences of a
# six-vector are penalized, through a 4 x 6 map.
D <- diff(diag(6), differences = 2)
curved <- quadratic_penalty(diag(4), map = D)
curved@n_coef
#> [1] 6
penalty_value(curved, 1:6, list(lambda = 1))
#> [1] 1.348774

# blocks = m repeats P without assembling I_m (x) P.
blocked <- quadratic_penalty(P, blocks = 4)
c(blocked@n_coef, penalty_rank(blocked))
#> [1] 20 12
all.equal(penalty_rank(blocked), 4L * penalty_rank(pen))
#> [1] TRUE
